_work.title: Majmūʻ fī al-falak — Collection on Timekeeping and Astronomical Instruments (Princeton, Garrett no. 3442Y)
_work.blurb: A composite Arabic codex of 19 distinct texts on timekeeping and astronomical instruments (Majmū' fī al-Falak), 125 leaves, spanning 1533–1667 CE, held at Princeton University Library (Garrett no. 3442Y). The collection gathers short treatises on the sine quadrant (rub' al-mujib), the solar quadrant, the horoscope (ahkam al-nujum), the sundial, and related astronomical calculation methods. The manuscript contains texts by multiple authors in nastaliq and naskh hands, along with zodiac classification tables, calendar correlation tables, and numeric calculation grids. The zodiac tables — which appear near the end of the codex alongside astrological treatises — organize the 12 zodiac signs by their elemental qualities (fire, water, air, earth), humoral correspondences, and calendar placements, making the manuscript a working reference for Islamic timekeeping and astrological practice. One table correlates Persian month names (Farvardin through Isfand) with the zodiac signs they fall in and the number of days in each. These tables are typical of the jadwal tradition of Islamic scientific manuscripts — compact, grid-form visual summaries of information otherwise scattered across prose texts.
_work.rights: Public Domain — 1533–1667 CE manuscript. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
_work.creator: Multiple authors (composite codex)

entries.title: Persian Calendar Months + Zodiac Signs Correspondence Table (Majmū' fī al-Falak, p. 44)
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A bordered jadwal (systematic table) from a Princeton composite astronomy codex (Garrett 3442Y) correlating the 12 Persian solar months with the zodiac signs (buruj) they fall in, along with day counts. The table is organized in a 5-column, 4-row grid: column headers give the Persian month names (from Farvardin/Aries through Isfand/Pisces — the 12 months of the Persian solar year as aligned with the zodiac), and each cell contains the Arabic name of the corresponding zodiac sign with the number of days. Visible zodiac signs include: Hamal (Aries), Thawr (Taurus), Jauza' (Gemini), Saratan (Cancer), Asad (Leo), Sunbulah (Virgo), Mawazin/Mizan (Libra), 'Aqrab (Scorpio), Qaws/Qawsiya (Sagittarius), Jadi (Capricorn), Dalw (Aquarius), Hut (Pisces). Day counts visible include 30, 31, 38 (likely a Persian calendar month crossing a zodiac boundary). The Persian solar year (Nowruz calendar) aligns closely with the zodiac because both are based on the Sun's position — making this table a conversion tool between Persian date-keeping and astrological zodiac position, essential for Islamic astronomers and astrologers who worked in both Persian and Arabic calendar systems simultaneously. The table is accompanied by a short prose text above and below explaining the context.

entries.title: Zodiac Signs Classification Table (Elemental Properties) — Majmū' fī al-Falak (p. 45)
entries.rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
entries.summary: A bordered jadwal (systematic reference table) from a Princeton composite astronomy codex (Garrett 3442Y) classifying the 12 zodiac signs by their qualitative properties — most likely their elemental attribution (fire/air/water/earth), their quality (hot/cold/wet/dry), their gender (masculine/feminine), and their other classification attributes used in Islamic astrological practice. The table is arranged as a bordered grid with Arabic zodiac sign names in cells organized by category rows and columns. Visible zodiac sign names include: 'Aqrab (Scorpio), Hamal (Aries), Asad (Leo), Jauza' (Gemini), Sunbulah (Virgo), Hut (Pisces), Jadi (Capricorn), Thawr (Taurus), Saratan (Cancer), and Mawazin (Libra). In Islamic astrology, the 12 zodiac signs are classified across multiple attribute systems simultaneously: the four elements (fire signs = Aries, Leo, Sagittarius; earth signs = Taurus, Virgo, Capricorn; air signs = Gemini, Libra, Aquarius; water signs = Cancer, Scorpio, Pisces), the triplicities, quadruplicities, hot/cold and wet/dry qualities, diurnal vs. nocturnal, and the four humors. The jadwal format encodes all of these classifications in a compact visual reference that the practitioner could consult while performing a horoscope calculation. This type of zodiac classification table is a standard feature of Arabic astrological handbooks from Ibn Rushd through Ottoman-era compilations, and its presence here (alongside the Persian calendar table on the preceding page) confirms that this section of the Garrett 3442Y codex functions as an astrological reference compendium.
